This tutorial covers test signals that carry their own **analytical ground
truth**. The motivating use case is benchmarking phasor, frequency and ROCOF
estimators (an estimator reports a value; we need to know the exact value it
*should* have reported), but the object is useful whenever you want a signal
whose amplitude, frequency and phase you know in closed form.

The `AnalyticSignal` object and the `build_analytic_signal` factory live in
`trimes.analytic` (numpy + pandas only). `trimes.synchrophasor` builds the
IEC/IEEE 60255-118-1 benchmark layer -- generators, the compliance test matrix,
TVE / FE / RFE metrics -- on top of it, and re-exports both names.

# The `AnalyticSignal` object

An `AnalyticSignal` wraps a sampled waveform (a pandas `Series`, exactly the
format the rest of *trimes* uses) together with three callables of a time
array:

* `amplitude(t)`   -- true peak amplitude of the fundamental,
* `frequency(t)`   -- true instantaneous frequency in Hz,
* `total_phase(t)` -- true total phase of the carrier in radians.

Because these are functions, the truth can be evaluated at **arbitrary**
instants -- not just the sample grid. That matters for estimators: a block
estimator timestamps its result at a window centre, a recursive one at the
current sample.

# Generators

The quickest way to get an `AnalyticSignal` is one of the generator functions.
They all take the sampling rate `fs` first and return an `AnalyticSignal`.

```{python}
from trimes.synchrophasor import steady_state, modulation, frequency_ramp

fs = 5_000.0
sig = steady_state(fs, nominal=50.0, frequency=50.2, amplitude=1.0, duration=0.2)
sig.signal.plot(grid=True, title=sig.signal.name)
```

`sig.signal` is the sampled waveform. Everything else is derived truth.

## Ground truth at arbitrary instants

`ground_truth(t)` returns a DataFrame with the columns an estimator trace has --
`frequency`, `amplitude`, `phase`, `rocof`, `phasor` -- evaluated at the instants
you pass (defaults to the sample grid).

```{python}
import numpy as np

# e.g. the window centres a 3-cycle block estimator would report at
report_times = np.arange(0.03, 0.2, 0.02)
truth = sig.ground_truth(report_times)
truth
```

The `phase` column is referenced to the nominal frequency and wrapped to
`[-pi, pi)`; since the tone is 0.2 Hz off nominal it rotates slowly. `phasor`
is the RMS complex phasor `(amplitude / sqrt(2)) * exp(1j * phase)`.

## A dynamic signal

`modulation` applies simultaneous amplitude and phase modulation (the IEEE /
IEC 60255-118-1 dynamic test). The frequency and ROCOF truth follow in closed
form.

```{python}
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

mod = modulation(fs, am_depth=0.1, pm_depth=0.1, modulation_frequency=2.0, duration=1.0)

t = mod.time
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(7, 5))
ax[0].plot(t, mod.signal.to_numpy());     ax[0].set_ylabel("signal")
ax[1].plot(t, mod.frequency(t));          ax[1].set_ylabel("frequency [Hz]")
ax[2].plot(t, mod.rocof(t));              ax[2].set_ylabel("ROCOF [Hz/s]")
for a in ax:
    a.grid(True)
```

ROCOF truth is a central difference of the frequency function with a `1e-4 s`
step -- for a piecewise-linear frequency that is exactly the mean of the
one-sided slopes at a corner.

## Frequency ramp and transition times

```{python}
ramp = frequency_ramp(fs, nominal=50.0, rocof=1.0, ramp_time=0.5, duration=1.0)
ramp.frequency(np.array([0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]))
```

Instants where the analytic model is not smooth are recorded in
`metadata["transition_times"]` -- here the two corners of the ramp. Phase 5
metrics use them to exclude frames around a disturbance from a compliance score.

```{python}
ramp.metadata["transition_times"]
```

# Building from your own callables

`build_analytic_signal` is the factory the generators are built on. Pass the
three truth callables and it samples the waveform straight from them
(`amplitude(t) * cos(total_phase(t))`, plus optional harmonics and seeded
noise), so the samples are exactly consistent with the truth.

```{python}
from trimes.analytic import build_analytic_signal

TWO_PI = 2 * np.pi
f0 = 50.0

# a linear amplitude sag, constant frequency
custom = build_analytic_signal(
    amplitude_fn=lambda t: np.where(t < 0.1, 1.0, 0.8),
    frequency_fn=lambda t: np.full_like(np.asarray(t, float), f0),
    total_phase_fn=lambda t: TWO_PI * f0 * np.asarray(t, float),
    fs=fs,
    duration=0.2,
    harmonics={5: 0.05},
    noise=0.01,
    seed=0,
    metadata={"transition_times": [0.1]},
)
custom.signal.plot(grid=True)
```

# Bridging from `PeriodicSignal`

The `PeriodicSignal` class from the signal-generation tutorial can hand back an
`AnalyticSignal` via `.analytic_signal()`, as long as its parameters have a
closed form -- a scalar frequency or a `(f_start, f_end)` ramp, a scalar or
ramped magnitude, zero offset and the default cosine carrier.

```{python}
from trimes.signal_generation import PeriodicSignal

t = np.arange(0.0, 0.2, 1 / fs)
ps = PeriodicSignal(t, f=(50.0, 52.0), mag=1.0)
asig = ps.analytic_signal(nominal=50.0)
asig.frequency(np.array([t[0], t[t.size // 2], t[-1]]))
```

# Concatenation with continuous truth

`superimpose_and_concat_analytic_signal` runs the same superimpose-and-concat
logic as `superimpose_and_concat_periodic_signals` (rows are superimposed,
segments concatenated) but also carries the **fundamental** phase across every
boundary and returns an `AnalyticSignal`. The fundamental is the first
`PeriodicSignal` of each row; the rest (harmonics, negative sequence) shape the
waveform but not the truth.

```{python}
from trimes.signal_generation import superimpose_and_concat_analytic_signal

mag = 110 * np.sqrt(2) / np.sqrt(3)
seg0 = np.arange(0.0, 0.1, 1 / fs)
seg1 = np.arange(0.1, 0.2, 1 / fs)
signals = [
    [PeriodicSignal(seg0, f=50.0, mag=mag), PeriodicSignal(seg0, f=250.0, mag=0.05 * mag)],
    [PeriodicSignal(seg1, f=52.0, mag=mag), PeriodicSignal(seg1, f=260.0, mag=0.05 * mag)],
]
concat = superimpose_and_concat_analytic_signal(signals, nominal=50.0)

t = concat.time
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(7, 4))
ax[0].plot(t, concat.signal.to_numpy()); ax[0].set_ylabel("signal")
ax[1].plot(t, concat.frequency(t));      ax[1].set_ylabel("frequency [Hz]")
for a in ax:
    a.grid(True)
```

The boundary where the fundamental frequency changes (50 to 52 Hz) is recorded:

```{python}
concat.metadata["transition_times"]
```

A deliberate angular jump can be injected at a boundary with `angular_jump`
(one value per interior boundary), which the truth respects.
```
